articles.title: No Thanksgiving cheer for markets as Europe gets set for another nervy session
articles.desc: Well, it was fun while it lasted, eh? After all the excitement surrounding Wall Street's rebound on Monday, we're back to some rather familiar territory heading into European trading today. The selloff in US tech stocks is resuming and there isn't much appetite to pick up the pieces just yet. After
articles.content: Well, it was fun while it lasted, eh? After all the excitement surrounding Wall Street's rebound on Monday, we're back to some rather familiar territory heading into European trading today. The selloff in US tech stocks is resuming and there isn't much appetite to pick up the pieces just yet. After the drop yesterday, S&P 500 futures are now down another 0.8% while Nasdaq futures are down 1.4% currently. So much for Jensen Huang coming to the rescue. And just to make things a little more uncomfortable for investors, US president Trump is stirring the tariffs pot again. Oh, how fun. But even without that, there are enough questions surrounding AI spending, stretched valuations and elevated Treasury yields to keep broader markets on their toes. And that has been the case for a few weeks already now. So, what can we extrapolate from the market mood in the past few sessions? The most telling thing is how quickly the enthusiasm from Monday has evaporated. The appetite for dip buying folded with sellers regaining control without much of a fight. So, that is the key takeaway for me. Over in the major currencies space, the dollar continues to keep firmer as well on the week. The early mover today though was the aussie as it had something to cheer about after another hot inflation report out of Australia. Trimmed mean inflation jumped to 3.8% in October, keeping the prospect of further RBA rate hikes alive. AUD/USD got a decent bump from that to 0.6660 but has since given back those gains and then some to 0.6590 now. So, where does all this leave us with heading into European trading later? Well, it's back to the same playbook as it has been all week I guess. Unless we get a fresh catalyst during the session, European traders might find themselves taking their cues from Wall Street once again. All eyes will be on the risk selloff and we're already seeing a more risk-off mood start to take hold. So, that will make for a bit of an ugly start to the morning in Europe. And with Thanksgiving coming tomorrow, do be mindful of thinner liquidity conditions in the second half of the week. With fewer traders around, even relatively modest orders can result in exacerbated price swings in market action. As such, I'd be wary of chasing any sharp rebounds under those circumstances. It's as good a time to be reminded that a sudden jump in stocks amid thinner holiday liquidity isn't quite the same thing as investors rediscovering their conviction to buy. As things stand, I would argue that the bulls might have to wait a little longer for their Thanksgiving feast. For now, it's the bears who are being served seconds. This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Lewisburg Avenue improvements to begin Jan. 4, 2027
articles.desc: FRANKLIN – The city has announced an updated schedule for the Lewisburg Avenue improvements project. Major construction will begin Jan. 4, 2027, and is expected to take one year to
articles.content: Lewisburg Avenue improvements to begin Jan. 4, 2027 | Local News | williamsonherald.com You have permission to edit this article. FRANKLIN – The city has announced an updated schedule for the Lewisburg Avenue improvements project. Major construction will begin Jan. 4, 2027, and is expected to take one year to complete. Lewisburg Avenue will be closed from Adams Street to Bonsal Way to accommodate installation of underground utilities. Throughout the project, the city will work closely with the contractor to reopen portions of the roadway and maintain access when it can be done safely. Lewisburg Avenue is an important corridor serving the downtown area. The project will improve pedestrian connectivity and upgrade the city’s infrastructure. Work includes installing new sidewalks, replacing existing underground utilities, building a new curb and gutter, installing a storm sewer system, and improving the railroad crossing on the corridor. The city chose a January start to coordinate with the downtown holiday event schedule. This allows community holiday events to take place as planned, while keeping the project on track for early in the new year. Before major construction begins, Atmos Energy will continue relocating natural gas utilities within the project limits. Crews will use temporary traffic flagging during this work, so drivers should expect occasional short delays. Please stay alert and follow posted traffic controls. This work will not require a full road closure. The construction contract allows 365 calendar days (one year) from the start of major construction. The city will work with the contractor and utility providers throughout the project and will share updates on construction activities and traffic impacts as they become available. For more information, visit the The city of Franklin appreciates the public’s patience and cooperation as these improvements move forward. The most widely recognized version of Ice Cream Cake is credited to Seed Junky Genetics, the Los Angeles breeder associated with a Wedding Cake × Gelato #33 cross. However, Mad Scientist Genetics has also developed a strain under the Ice Cream Cake name, using Cheesecake × Dream Cookie genetics. These differing parentage accounts demonstrate why a familiar strain name does not necessarily identify a single genetic lineage. Understanding Ice Cream Cake's Conflicting Genetics Seed Junky Genetics' Ice Cream Cake gained attention during the rise of dessert-named cannabis strains in 2019. The Wedding Cake and Gelato #33 cross became widely referenced in strain databases and breeder descriptions. However, the separate Cheesecake × Dream Cookie version from Mad Scientist Genetics complicates efforts to assign one definitive pedigree to everything sold under the Ice Cream Cake name. Historical laboratory records identify β-caryophyllene and limonene as the leading terpenes, each with a reported median of approximately 0.41%, followed by β-myrcene at approximately 0.24%. articles.title: Radiant scales Kaleidos production
articles.desc: Radiant Industries has announced a $380m manufacturing expansion across California and Tennessee to accelerate production of its Kaleidos microreactor.
articles.content: ​​​Radiant scales Kaleidos production - Nuclear Engineering International Radiant Industries has announced a $380m dual-site manufacturing expansion in California and Tennessee to move its Kaleidos nuclear microreactor into commercial production ahead of initial customer deliveries targeted for 2028. In El Segundo, California Radiant is investing over $100m in a new headquarters and to add roughly 200,000 square feet of manufacturing and R&D space. The facility includes bridge cranes, control-system testing infrastructure, and in-house turbomachinery production to assemble multiple reactors in parallel. In Oak Ridge, Tennessee, Radiant is investing $280m into an 81-acre campus where construction is underway for its R-50 fuelling and high-rate production facility, which is scheduled to begin fuelling operations in 2027. It will allow Radiant to load fuel privately and ship factory-sealed, plug-in-ready reactors, eliminating the need for customers to perform on-site nuclear construction. Long-term staffing is projected to exceed 300 employees. “Our El Segundo headquarters strengthens the connection between engineering, innovation and manufacturing, while our Oak Ridge factory establishes the infrastructure to produce and fuel Kaleidos at commercial scale,” said Tori Shivanandan, President and COO of Radiant. “Together, these facilities represent a major investment in American nuclear manufacturing and position Radiant to meet growing military and commercial demand and deliver the world’s first factory-built, truck-transportable 1 MW commercial nuclear microreactor at scale.” Dr Rita Baranwal, Chief Nuclear Officer of Radiant, noted: “By building our fuelling capabilities first and expanding manufacturing in phases, we’re putting the infrastructure in place to support initial customer deliveries and scale production as demand increases.” Kaleidos is a transportable, high-temperature gas-cooled microreactor using helium coolant and TRIstructural ISOtropic (TRISO) fuel, designed to fit inside a single shipping container. It generates 3 MWt (1 MWe) and runs for about five years before refuelling. Radiant’s first unit, built in El Segundo, is undergoing full-scale testing at the Idaho National Laboratory (INL) DOME facility, having received Department of Energy (DOE) approval for its Documented Safety Analysis in late October. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) accepted Radiant’s 10 CFR Part 70 licence application for accelerated review, targeting completion in January 2027. Fuel supply agreements are secured with DOE, Centrus Energy, Urenco, and Standard Nuclear. The US Army awarded Radiant up to $750m to develop and deploy 15 Kaleidos units under the , with initial delivery planned for 2028 and all 15 units expected to be deployed by 2030, including deployment at Fort Benning, Georgia. The Department of the Air Force has selected Radiant to develop and operate a microreactor at Buckley Space Force Base in Aurora, Colorado while the Department of the Navy has selected the company to supply energy to the Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana. articles.title: Holiday Flyers Will Forgive a Crying Baby — But Not Kids Who Do This
articles.desc: A new survey shows what frequent flyers will actually speak up about on planes, from seat-kicking kids to seat swaps, ahead of the Thanksgiving travel rush.
articles.content: Holiday Flyers Will Forgive a Crying Baby — But Not Kids Who Do This Holiday Flyers Will Forgive a Crying Baby — But Not Kids Who Do This hanksgiving week in the US usually sends a rush of travelers through US airports, and the Sunday after Thanksgiving is usually the busiest travel day on any given year. In fact, TSA says it’s estimating it will screen more than nationwide on Sunday, Nov. 29. That would put it just shy of the same Sunday in 2025, when it screened 3.13 million people — an all-time record for the agency. Those 3 million flyers will be a mix of kids, grandparents, frequent flyers, and maybe-once-a-year flyers, so some friction between travelers is all but guaranteed. , a platform for finding flights using loyalty points, looked at how frequent flyers handle the friction that comes with a packed flight. The company’s 2026 airplane etiquette survey talked to 2,018 travelers, more than half of whom reported flying at least five times a year. Other similar surveys have found that seat-kicking is the single most annoying in-flight behavior , but the point.me survey asked a slightly different question: not what bothers frequent flyers, but what they’ll actually speak up about. dreading how their fellow passengers will respond to their crying infant can relax a little: only 2.3 percent of respondents said they would speak up about a crying baby — perhaps because everyone understands there’s very little to be done about it. Older kids are another matter, however. More than 80 percent of people said they would speak up about an older child kicking their seat, making it the most likely behavior on the list to get a reaction. More than half (55.5 percent) would speak up about someone playing audio without headphones, and 45.8 percent would say something to a neighbor taking over their already limited legroom. Men said they were more willing to confront fellow passengers across the board. More than 85 percent of men would address a seat-kicker, compared to just 73.9 percent of women. About 60 percent of men said they would call out audio played without headphones, compared with 50.7 percent of women. Men were also more likely to step in if someone was rude to a flight attendant, at 34.7 percent versus 26.4 percent of women. The window-versus-aisle debate has a gender split, too. Women were split almost evenly between the window (35.1 percent) and the aisle (34.8 percent), while men clearly favored the aisle (41.8 percent). Gen Z was the only age group that preferred the window on the whole, with 45 percent opting for it. But the dreaded middle seat actually wasn’t chosen as the least-favorite option. That honor went to the seat next to the bathrooms, with 41.9 percent saying it was their least favorite. The next worst seat was the middle, but not just any middle: 38.1 percent said their least favorite is the middle seat of a wide-body plane’s middle row of five. Thanksgiving flights are full of families trying to sit together, but the survey showed getting someone to swap seats isn’t a guarantee. The most popular reason people gave for agreeing to change seats was that the new one was in a better location (57.5 percent of respondents). A generous 57.2 percent said they’d agree to swap simply to help a parent sit with a young child. After that, goodwill dropped off. Only 33.4 percent said they would swap so a family could sit together, and fewer (28.5 percent) would do it to allow a couple to sit together. Another 12.1 percent said it’s never acceptable to ask a stranger to swap seats. The takeaway for families traveling together, especially during busy travel days, is to spend the extra money to book seats together rather than counting on the kindness of a stranger at the gate. Sixty-two percent of respondents said they use the call button to get a flight attendant’s attention. But younger travelers were far more likely to avoid asking for help at all. articles.title: Meta Muse can now shop Walmart's Black Friday deals on your behalf
articles.desc: Walmart lets Meta's Muse AI shop Black Friday deals starting November 23, requiring a spending cap and approval via new Agent Profiles.
articles.content: Meta Muse can now shop Walmart's Black Friday deals on your behalf Walmart is opening its online store to Meta's Muse AI agent, letting the assistant find and buy Black Friday deals on your behalf. The integration goes live through Walmart's Sparky AI assistant and the new , a system the retailer announced last month that lets AI agents search for products without accessing your purchase history. Muse operates through "Agent Profiles," a dedicated space within your Walmart customer account. These profiles let you set spending limits, approve purchases, and review everything the agent buys. Walmart confirmed the rollout after a brief delay, with the feature available starting November 23rd. The shopping process follows three steps. First, you tell Muse what you need - for example, asking it to find a TV deal or show available Black Friday offers. Muse explores products and builds your basket. Next, you sign into Walmart through Muse and create an Agent Profile, which includes setting a spending cap you're comfortable with. Finally, you complete the purchase within the conversation using a card saved in your Walmart account. Walmart said prices match what you would find on Walmart.com, and the company's standard return policy still applies to agent-made purchases. Walmart's move stands in contrast to competitors. Amazon and eBay have both blocked AI agents from browsing their platforms. Walmart said Meta's Muse is "just the beginning," with additional shopping experiences for other AI agents and apps "on the way." For professionals tracking how AI agents reshape commerce, this signals a shift from experimental access to live, transactional deployment. Understanding agent architectures and integration patterns is becoming a practical skill - not just a technical curiosity. offer structured paths for teams building or managing these systems. Why this matters for sales, marketing, and product teams For sales and marketing professionals, Walmart's decision to welcome AI agents rather than block them creates a new purchase channel. Agents that can browse, compare, and transact change how customers discover products. Marketing teams will need to consider how their product data appears to non-human shoppers, while product development teams face decisions about making catalogs machine-readable. Customer support and finance teams also have a stake. Agent Profiles introduce spending limits and approval workflows, which means customer service staff may field questions about agent-made purchases. Finance departments will track spending that originates from AI assistants rather than direct human action - a new line item in procurement and expense management. Hospitality and events professionals managing seasonal purchasing may find agents useful for bulk orders, provided the guardrails are set correctly.

articles.title: Spotify Outage Hits New York Users, Nearly 15,000 Report Login Trouble
articles.desc: Nearly 15,000 Downdetector reports flagged Spotify login failures in New York and beyond Tuesday, with most users unable to sign back in.
articles.content: Spotify Outage Hits New York Users Tuesday Morning Spotify Outage Hits New York Users, Nearly 15,000 Report Login Trouble Spotify users across New York spent part of Tuesday morning locked out of their own accounts, as reports of the music streaming platform going haywire piled up fast. Nearly 15,000 user reports hit Downdetector as of 6:35 a.m. EST, with most people describing the same frustrating loop: logged out, and unable to log back in. , which reported that New York-area Spotify users were among those hit by the disruption, according to Downdetector tracking. The outlet noted that most of the people reporting trouble said they had been signed out of the app and simply could not get back in. The timing lines up with a broader spike that TechRadar tracked starting around 6:15 a.m. ET, when outage reports suddenly jumped on Downdetector. By the time the site's live coverage had updated, U.S. reports had climbed past 16,500, with more than 8,000 additional reports logged in the U.K., according to . Earlier in the morning, the same outlet had put the counts at just over 10,000 in the U.S. and over 4,500 in the U.K., showing how quickly the numbers grew. It wasn't just a login problem for some users. TechRadar reported that thousands of people also said they couldn't play music they had downloaded for offline listening, on top of being unable to sign in at all. Spotify's own Status account acknowledged the trouble, confirming the company was aware of “today's issues” and was checking them out, per the same report. A breakdown of the complaint types, reported by sundayguardianlive.com, found that 68 percent of the issues were tied to login problems, while 29 percent involved trouble with the Spotify app itself, and the remaining 2 percent were linked to server connection issues. That same report noted a wrinkle: Spotify's official status page was showing “All Systems Operational” with no incident listed for the day, even as user complaints mounted elsewhere. Tuesday's disruption wasn't an isolated incident for the streaming giant. Sundayguardianlive.com noted that Spotify dealt with a major outage in September, when the company acknowledged login problems and said it was investigating. Status monitoring records also showed several shorter disruptions throughout October involving app loading and connectivity, according to the same report, suggesting Tuesday's trouble fits a pattern rather than a one-off glitch. For now, it remains unclear what caused Tuesday's disruption or how long the login troubles persisted for affected users in New York and elsewhere. What is clear is that thousands of listeners, mid-commute or mid-playlist, found themselves locked out of their music library. articles.content: Scientists Simulated What May Happen If a Nuclear Bomb Goes Off in Space. The Fallout Is Terrifying. | United States Scientists Simulated What May Happen If a Nuclear Bomb Goes Off in Space. The Fallout Is Terrifying. Detonating a nuclear bomb in space would wipe out 98% of our satellites—and the tech that relies on them. orbiting Earth should be an obvious sign that intelligent life exists on this planet. The problem is that an alien spacecraft might be better off keeping its distance. As the spiral into dystopia here on Earth continues, there has been growing concern that someone could take out many of those satellites with aWhen a team of researchers from Princeton and the University of Wisconsin-Madison gauged the theoretical destruction of a nuclear strike in, the results were grim. There have been over 13,000 satellites at altitudes under 1,242 miles since early 2026. Scientists Have 'Resurrected' 12 Coral Species on The Great Barrier Reef Many of these fly close together in a region of about 193-232 square miles , and the use of LEO has only been expanding as the U.S. Department of Defense cmore for detecting missiles and carrying out military communications, but they have only become more of a target for hostile forces. In an unnerving thought experiment, the researchers worked out the aftermath of detonating a one-megaton nuclear weapon 311 miles above the South Atlantic—they found it would easily wipe out about 98% of satellites. “Radiation-disabled spacecraft remain in orbit but are assumed to lose maneuverability,” they said in a study recently posted to the preprint server. “We follow collisions and breakup fragments in altitude bands, retaining mass and allowing fragments to move above and below their birth altitude after a velocity kick. Both intact objects and debris descend under atmospheric drag. ” This is not the first time a “what if” like has been batted around, in theory or otherwise. Nuclear paranoia decades ago led to an actual experiment that revealed the potential horrors of detonating something in LEO. On July 9, 1962, the thesaw a 1.4-megaton bomb detonated in the Pacific, around 400 km above Johnston Atoll. An artificial radiation belt was created by clouds of electrons released from radioactive debris scattered by nuclear fission. It caused severe damage to satellites that were either in outfit at the time or launched soon afterward. Radiation continues to be dangerous long after the initial explosion, because spacecraft continue to pass through it as they orbit, experiencing degrading effects that make them more difficult to maneuver. They then end up at increased risk of collision. , which would disable 25% of the fleet in not even a day. That would rocket to 78% after three days and 98% after a week. Damaged satelliteswould collide with each other—or scraps of space junk—and gradually shut down services that rely on them. There would be three collisions within 15 days and double that by 30. Smashing spacecraft would also clog LEO with fragments that would put even more satellites at risk, and at least 19 collisions would occur a year after the detonation. Atmospheric drag would reduce the hazard by removing disabled spacecraft orbiting lower, but those at higher altitudes would remain at the highest risk. Disabled satellites would continue to die off. Starfish Prime was so disastrous that the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty was signed by the U.S. and the Soviet Union a year later. This enforced an outright ban on testing nuclear weapons anywhere but underground, whether it was on the surface, in the atmosphere, or deep in space. Satellites in LEO have multiplied since the 1960s. How long radioactive ions can keep letting electrons loose above the atmosphere is still uncertain, but satellite breakdowns would be staggering.
